Thank you for organizing this workshop. I found several questions challenging to answer due to the complexities involved in balancing privacy and effectiveness. For instance, Q3.4 on Absalon data was particularly tough because while it might improve identification, the invasion of privacy is a significant concern.

I believe the most critical questions are those around explainability (Q4) and fairness (Q5). Understanding why a student is flagged as struggling is crucial for providing appropriate support, and ensuring the model works equally well across different groups is essential to avoid perpetuating inequalities. One notable point of divergence in our responses was Q3.6.nationality, where I lean towards "only if it improves fairness." This approach ensures that the model does not inadvertently disadvantage certain groups.

Opt-out mechanisms could be a way to address some privacy concerns while still allowing the model to function effectively.

Thank you for this opportunity. I found Q3.4 challenging because Absalon data feels intrusive, but I understand its potential benefits. The most important questions are about explainability and fairness. For me, high explainability is crucial to build trust.

I noticed a divergence in opinions on Q3.5.disability. I chose "no_threshold" because disability-related information should not be used unless necessary, as it might inadvertently disadvantage students like myself with dyslexia. An opt-out mechanism could help ensure that students who are uncomfortable with data collection can still receive support if needed.

Thank you for this workshop.

I found Q3.5 regarding sensitive data particularly challenging because of the ethical dilemmas involved. For example, while I see the potential benefits of using financial aid status to improve identification (Q3.5.financial_aid), I also recognize the privacy concerns and potential stigma associated with it. I chose "small" improvement threshold for this data because I believe the potential benefit of identifying struggling students early justifies its use under strict privacy safeguards.

The most important questions for me are those around fairness (Q5). Ensuring that the model works equally well across different groups is crucial to avoid perpetuating inequalities. I noticed a divergence in opinions on Q3.6.nationality, where many chose "never" acceptable. As an advisor, I believe that if nationality data can improve fairness, it should be considered with careful safeguards and transparency.

An opt-out mechanism could help address some of the concerns raised about sensitive data use, allowing students to choose their level of participation while still benefiting from the support system.

I noticed a divergence in opinions on Q3.6.first_gen, where many chose "only if it improves fairness." I agree because first-gen students might need extra support, but using this data should not lead to stereotyping or unfair assumptions. An opt-out mechanism could help balance privacy concerns with the model's effectiveness.
